question: A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of progressive shortness of breath and intermittent cough with blood-tinged sputum. During this time, he has also noticed blood in his urine. He has no history of serious illness and does not take any medications. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows crackles at both lung bases. Urinalysis is positive for blood and results of a direct enzyme-linked immunoassay are positive for anti-GBM antibodies. The pathogenesis of this patient's disease is most similar to which of the following?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Anti-GBM antibodies" -> "attack glomerular basement membrane" -> "glomerulonephritis" -> "lung hemorrhage" -> "Goodpasture syndrome" -> "similar to autoimmune hemolytic anemia" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Anti-GBM antibodies" -> "bind to basement membrane" -> "complement activation" -> "tissue damage" -> "similar to autoimmune hemolytic anemia" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Anti-GBM antibodies" -> "immune complex formation" -> "glomerular inflammation" -> "pulmonary hemorrhage" -> "similar to autoimmune hemolytic anemia" -> 75%
enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms and positive anti-GBM antibodies indicate Goodpasture syndrome, characterized by glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage due to antibodies targeting the glomerular basement membrane. This pathogenesis involves direct antibody binding and complement activation, leading to tissue damage, similar to the mechanism in autoimmune hemolytic anemia where antibodies target red blood cells. The retrieved evidence paths confirm the pulmonary involvement and glomerulonephritis as manifestations of anti-GBM disease, aligning with the consensus that Goodpasture syndrome shares a similar autoimmune mechanism with autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Other options like Henoch-Schönlein purpura, polyarteritis nodosa, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, and graft versus host disease involve different immunological processes and are not directly comparable in pathogenesis to Goodpasture syndrome.
analysis: The patient's presentation of hemoptysis, hematuria, and positive anti-GBM antibodies is indicative of Goodpasture syndrome. This condition is characterized by the presence of antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane, leading to glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. The pathogenesis involves direct antibody binding to a specific target, similar to the mechanism seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where antibodies target red blood cells. Both conditions involve an autoimmune process where antibodies directly attack specific components of the body, leading to tissue damage. Other options, such as Henoch-Schönlein purpura, polyarteritis nodosa, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, and graft versus host disease, involve different immunological mechanisms, such as immune complex deposition or T-cell mediated responses, and are not directly comparable to the antibody-mediated process seen in Goodpasture syndrome. Therefore, the pathogenesis of Goodpasture syndrome is most similar to that of autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
